name: Normalcy Bias
description: People can discount warning signs and assume an abnormal situation will stay manageable because 'things are probably still normal.' In practice the label is used most often for delayed action around disasters, crises, or emergencies.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to crisis UX, fraud/security prompts, climate/safety messaging, and incident communications: users may downplay abnormal warnings or postpone action because the situation still feels ordinary enough to ignore.
myth_risk_note: Updated 2026-09-07: myth risk stays moderate. The construct has a real academic origin and definition, but no controlled experimental demonstration of the bias's occurrence or magnitude exists yet -- popular usage likely overstates how settled this is as a tested psychological effect versus a clinical-theory construct.
prevalence_note: Widely recognized in emergency-management and risk-communication discourse, especially after large crises, but still not a routine named heuristic in mainstream day-to-day product design practice.

findings.description: Introduces and defines "normalcy bias" as a real construct in disaster-response psychology: the tendency to underestimate the probability or extent of expected disruption because it hasn't happened before, contrasted with an "abnormalcy bias" (underestimating victims' own coping ability). This is a genuine, peer-reviewed theoretical grounding for the construct's existence and definition in clinical/disaster-response literature, but the paper is conceptual -- it does not report an experiment measuring the bias's occurrence or magnitude.
findings.effect_size: Not applicable -- theoretical/clinical framework paper, no measured effect
findings.source_title: The continuity principle: A unified approach to disaster and trauma
